title: Minecraft’s reclusive creator has a proposition for Anthropic
excerpt: Minecraft creator Markus Persson asked Anthropic in a post on X if he could get "more unlimited token usage and perhaps even more speed."
content_html:
By Natalie Musumeci

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-26T10:49:01.260Z

Minecraft creator Markus Persson has a request for Anthropic: He wants more AI power — and he's willing to pay.

"@AnthropicAI Yo, any chance I could get more unlimited token usage and perhaps even more speed?" the billionaire video game developer, commonly known as "Notch," wrote in a Monday X post.

"I've got the money to burn, and I'd love to exchange it for better goods and services. And I'm building new shit that I've never seen before," Persson said.

Persson also expressed support for the AI giant's approach to the rapidly advancing technology, writing, "I agree with your AI manifesto, btw."

Elon Musk was apparently amused by Persson's post, replying to it with a laughing emoji.

@AnthropicAI Yo, any chance I could get more unlimited token usage and perhaps even more speed? I've got the money to burn, and I'd love to exchange it for better goods and services. And I'm building new shit that I've never seen before. I agree with your AI manifesto, btw.

— notch (@notch) November 23, 2026

Persson's appeal to Anthropic, the newly public company behind the Claude AI chatbot, marks a turnabout for the Minecraft creator. Persson was once fiercely opposed to using AI for coding.

At the beginning of the year, he called it an "incredibly bad idea still" and said, "anyone advocating for it is either incompetent or evil."

By July, Persson said he was trying out coding with AI, and a month later he said it might be time to "eat some crow."

"One of the reasons I don't want to embrace this AI thing too much is that I'd prefer to stay a developer and not become middle management," Persson wrote in an August post. "Feels related somehow."

Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment about Persson's proposition.

Her coverage often focused on stories at the intersection of law, business, politics, and technology. Natalie has covered Donald Trump’s criminal and civil cases, the wave of lawsuits against the second Trump administration, the indictment and criminal trial of Sean “Diddy” Combs, the shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, and the legal battles facing Elon Musk and his companies. Natalie came to Business Insider in June 2021 as a breaking news reporter, focusing on the most interesting angles on the day's trending news. Natalie largely drove BI’s coverage around the fatal “Rust” shooting involving Alec Baldwin and the disappearance and murder of Gabby Petito.Prior to joining BI, Natalie worked for the New York Post, the New York Daily News, and The Brooklyn Paper. She has an extensive background covering crime and courts. During her more than 12-year journalism career, she did a stint covering the police beat out of the New York Police Department's headquarters. Natalie, a Brooklyn native, graduated from Brooklyn College in 2012 with a degree in journalism.
